insights.summary: Oil prices face a deferred — not eliminated — upside shock, with the base case being elevated prices that only gradually decline if geopolitics stabilize. Three specific triggers could reignite a sharp move higher.
insights.key_reasoning: A temporary buffer from pre-disruption Iranian shipments afloat and China's government-directed demand suppression has delayed — not resolved — the underlying supply risk; depletion of strategic reserves and infrastructure damage could accelerate the move.

insights.summary: China's oil import policy is identified as one of the single biggest near-term price drivers; a resumption of normal or elevated Chinese crude imports would be a significant bullish catalyst for oil.
insights.key_reasoning: China has used command-economy tools to artificially suppress oil consumption and imports; any policy reversal or demand normalization removes a key bearish offset currently keeping prices lower.

insights.summary: Refined product prices (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel) are likely to remain structurally elevated relative to crude due to persistent damage to Russian refining infrastructure, supporting refining-margin-exposed assets.

insights.summary: Permanent or prolonged destruction of energy infrastructure (pipelines, refineries, Gulf/Russian production facilities) represents a tail-risk scenario that could sustain oil price increases for months to years.
insights.key_reasoning: Unlike shipping disruptions which are temporary, physical destruction of production or refining infrastructure creates multi-year supply deficits that cannot be quickly offset by reserve releases or demand adjustments.
insights.notable_data: Supply losses from infrastructure destruction described as potentially lasting 'months or even years'

insights.key_reasoning: Global SPRs are already described as relatively low after prior drawdowns; further depletion means governments have diminished capacity to offset future supply shocks, amplifying price volatility.

insights.summary: Nvidia and AI semiconductor names are currently benefiting from an accounting timing tailwind — revenue is booked immediately upon chip sales while buyers spread costs over years — but this 'golden window' is finite and reversal risk rises as depreciation catches up.
insights.key_reasoning: Chip sellers book profit immediately while buyers capitalize the cost, creating a simultaneous earnings boom on both sides of the transaction that is structurally temporary; as capex growth decelerates post-2026 and depreciation waves hit, the earnings growth story for semis narrows.
